species_boxplots.png.caption: Amplitude, width, recovery, fall time and the steep part of the fall of every pool drop (the 24 Nov auto-detect pool: drops nobody has judged or been shown), one box per recording, recordings grouped by species. Box: the middle half; line: the median; whiskers: the 5th to 95th percentile; dots: every drop. Log scales. Width and recovery exist only where the drop climbed half-way back before the next drop or two hours (last panel: how often that happened, and how often the fall ran on as a long tail). The fall time runs from the top to the bottom, so it includes a slow shoulder or tail; the steep part is the fall's fast core alone.

species_rainclouds.png.caption: The same drops, one row per species: the shaded hill is how the values are spread (a smoothed histogram of the log values), the box the middle half, the dots the drops. The number is the median.

species_width_amplitude.png.caption: Width against amplitude. Small panels: one species each (grey: every other drop), coloured by recording. Large panel: the region holding the densest half (filled) and 90 % (thin line) of each species' drops. Part 1 of 2: oyster, chocolate oyster, snow oyster, lion's mane, Asian shiitake, split gill (the figure has room for six species; the grey is this part's drops).

species_fall_vs_recovery.png.caption: Is a drop fast down and slow up? Left: fall time against the time to climb half-way back. On the dashed line a drop recovers as fast as it fell. Right: the ratio, one row per species.

species_typical_shape.png.caption: Every drop stretched to the same size (its amplitude becomes 1) and the same duration (its fall time, left, or its width, right), then the median across each species. Bands: the middle half of the drops. Left, after 1 the line shows how far each species climbs back in the time it took to fall.

map_width_medoids.png.caption: The plane cut into cells that split in four while they hold more than 36 drops, so the grid is finest where drops crowd. Each cell with at least 5 drops shows its medoid (its most typical real drop), each drop first divided by its own amplitude (the glyph's height is the same everywhere; its place on the map gives its size). The glyph runs from half a cell-width before the top to 2.5 after; the thin line is the level of the top. Colour along the medoid: blue where the cell's drops agree, red where they differ. Grey band: their middle half. Grey dots: cells too sparse for a waveform. Drops beyond the 0.5th / 99.5th percentile sit on the edge cells. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

map_width_medoids_zoom.png.caption: The same map, zoomed on the region of its finest cells, where the glyphs are too small to read on the whole map. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

map_width_heatmaps.png.caption: The same cells, but each glyph is a heat map of ALL the cell's drops overlaid (dark blue where many traces pass, white where none do), each time-column scaled to its own total; orange: the cell's median trace. A sharp dark line means the cell's drops share one shape; a smear means they differ. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

map_width_cells.png.caption: Left: the drops and the cells of the adaptive grid. Right: each cell coloured by the species most of its drops come from, pale where the species mix; the number is its drop count. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

map_fall_medoids.png.caption: The plane cut into cells that split in four while they hold more than 36 drops, so the grid is finest where drops crowd. Each cell with at least 5 drops shows its medoid (its most typical real drop), each drop first divided by its own amplitude (the glyph's height is the same everywhere; its place on the map gives its size). The glyph runs from half a cell-width before the top to 5 after; the thin line is the level of the top. Colour along the medoid: blue where the cell's drops agree, red where they differ. Grey band: their middle half. Grey dots: cells too sparse for a waveform. Drops beyond the 0.5th / 99.5th percentile sit on the edge cells. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

map_fall_medoids_zoom.png.caption: The same map, zoomed on the region of its finest cells, where the glyphs are too small to read on the whole map. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

map_fall_heatmaps.png.caption: The same cells, but each glyph is a heat map of ALL the cell's drops overlaid (dark blue where many traces pass, white where none do), each time-column scaled to its own total; orange: the cell's median trace. A sharp dark line means the cell's drops share one shape; a smear means they differ. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

map_fall_cells.png.caption: Left: the drops and the cells of the adaptive grid. Right: each cell coloured by the species most of its drops come from, pale where the species mix; the number is its drop count. Drawn from a random sample of 30,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops: each cell's medoid compares every drop in it with every other.

grid10_fall_amplitude_shaded.png.caption: The fall-time map again, on a uniform 10 x 10 grid (equal steps on log scales between the 1st and 99th percentiles; the edge cells hold everything beyond). Each cell shows its medoid, the most typical real drop, divided by its own amplitude, from half a column-width before its top to 5 after, and the middle half of its drops behind it. Each cell is shaded by the share of all drops it holds (a probability map); the medoid is coloured blue where the cell's drops agree and red where they differ.

grid10_fall_amplitude_opacity.png.caption: The fall-time map again, on a uniform 10 x 10 grid (equal steps on log scales between the 1st and 99th percentiles; the edge cells hold everything beyond). Each cell shows its medoid, the most typical real drop, divided by its own amplitude, from half a column-width before its top to 5 after, and the middle half of its drops behind it. Each waveform's darkness and thickness follow how many drops the cell holds, so the common shapes stand out and the rare ones fade.

grid10_steepness_recovery_shaded.png.caption: Two measures that do not depend on how long a drop lasts. Down the grid: steepness - how many times steeper the fall's steepest moment is than its average slope (top: gentle straight ramps; bottom: sudden cliffs). Across: how long the drop took to climb half-way back, divided by how long it took to fall (left: quick recoveries, V shapes; right: slow ones; last column: never climbed half-way back). Every drop is scaled to its own fall time (the fall runs from 0 to 1 of the glyph's time) and its own amplitude, so the glyphs show shape alone. Line: the cell's median drop; white band: its middle half; cell shading: how common the cell is.

grid10_steepness_recovery_opacity.png.caption: The same steepness-by-recovery grid, without shading: each waveform's darkness and thickness follow how many drops its cell holds, so the common shapes stand out and the rare ones fade.

grid10_steepness_position_shaded.png.caption: Down: steepness (gentle ramps at the top, cliffs at the bottom). Across: where in the fall the drop happens - the moment it is half-way down, as a fraction of its fall time (left: it plunges at once and then creeps; middle: an even fall; right: it creeps first and plunges at the end). The glyphs show two fall times after the top, so the fall itself fills the left part of each glyph.

grid10_position_recovery_shaded.png.caption: Down: where in the fall the drop happens (bottom row: it plunges at once; top row: it creeps and then plunges at the end). Across: recovery time divided by fall time (last column: never climbed half-way back). Each glyph is the cell's median drop scaled to its own fall time and amplitude.

species_fingerprints.png.caption: Each species' fingerprint - the region holding the densest half of its drops - for six pairs of measures. Top: amplitude against fall time and against recovery, and fall time against recovery. Bottom: the time-free shape measures - steepness (how sudden the fall is), recovery time over fall time, and where in the fall the drop happens. Where the shapes separate, the species drop differently; where they overlap, the measure does not tell them apart.

extra/drop_raster.png.caption: Every pool drop as a tick on its channel's timeline, coloured by amplitude. Gaps are stretches where the pool's rules kept no drop: stretches already reviewed or queued, noisy ones, and quiet ones.

extra/size_distributions.png.caption: For each size x, the share of drops at least that big, on log-log axes. A curve that bends down steeply has a typical size; a long straight run would mean sizes with no typical scale (as in avalanches). The review sample and the noise floor shape the small end, so read the middle and the tail.

extra/shape_space.png.caption: Every drop scaled to the same width and amplitude, then compared. Top left: the two directions in which the shapes differ most (principal components). Top middle and right: a t-SNE map, which places drops of similar shape near each other. Bottom: what moving along each component does to the average drop. Drawn from a random sample of 20,000 of the pool's 131,651 drops (t-SNE grows with the square of the drops it places).

anatomy_example.png.caption: One ordinary drop with its measures. Amplitude: the top to the bottom. Fall time: the top to the bottom. Width: the top to the moment it has climbed back half of the amplitude. Recovery: the bottom to that moment. The whole-drop rule (79d0243e) finds the top and the bottom; every figure here uses it.
